newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Bosnian Serb president to swear in new army chief.
newsitem.headline: Bosnian Serb president to swear in new army chief.

text.p: Bosnian Serb President Biljana Plavsic was to lead a swearing-in ceremony for her new military commander and his deputy on Sunday, completing a manoeuvre to oust indicted war criminal Ratko Mladic as army chief.
The Bosnian Serb news agency SRNA said on Saturday Plavsic had "restructured" the army's General Headquarters and appointed a new commander and deputy.
Because of "the well-known stand of the international community" Plavsic said she was unable to name the 52-year-old career soldier Mladic as new Chief of the Army Headquarters.
The statement appeared to confirm weeks of speculation in the Belgrade media that a purge of the Serb military's top brass had taken place.
One independent weekly newspaper said as many as 80 of Mladic's top officers and advisers would be pensioned off, including his chief-of-staff, and heads of the military intelligence services.
International mediators in Sarajevo were cautiously pleased. One U.S. embassy official said the move was "a good first step that should have been taken a long time ago".
Figures like international High Representative Carl Bildt have long been demanding that Mladic be extradited to a tribunal in The Hague to answer charges of war crimes and genocide.
He is accused of directing the siege of Sarajevo and overseeing the massacre of some 8,000 unarmed Moslems from the enclave of Srebrenica in eastern Bosnia last year.

But diplomats who have watched the Serbs repeatedly thumb their noses at world opinion say the purge probably has less to do with Western pressure than a long-running and increasingly public feud among political and military leaders.

Last week, the head of the Bosnian Serb military's information service General Manilo Milutinovic published an open letter in a Belgrade news magazine, listing a series of grievances over the way the politicians ran the war including alleged profiteering.
The letter indicated the dispute had its roots early in the war -- the military loyal to the leftist administration in Belgrade at odds with the right-wing Serb nationalist party leaders.
It flared last year when the former Bosnian Serb president Radovan Karadzic unsuccessfully tried to fire Mladic, who accused the politicians of treason and war profiteering.
NATO and Western mediators said they were adopting a "wait and see" approach to the latest reports of dismissal.

Bildt's spokesman Colum Murphy said it was too early to tell who would win this round: "(Bildt) thinks it's a little premature and is waiting to see what comes out of this particular move by Madame Plavsic."

Bosnian Serb military sources also indicated that Mladic and his staff had not given up the battle. By late on Saturday night they were still meeting in their headquarters at Han Pijesak to discuss the forced "retirements".

But Plavsic appeared confident that her strategy would work. Her defence minister Milan Ninkovic introduced the new army chief, Major General Pero Colic, to Bildt's military advisor on Saturday afternoon.
And in a move clearly intended to undercut Mladic's powerbase, Bosnian Serb TV quoted Ninkovic as saying the army headquarters had been moved from Han Pijesak to Pale -- the Serb political seat.
What was not clear was how the Serb public would react to the struggle.
Serbs revered Mladic as a folk hero for his audacious front-line leadership. A genuine fighting soldier, the burly, bull-necked Mladic commanded in the front line alongside his men.

He won respect or fear from his foes through a mixture of bluff, breathtaking disregard for human life and force of personality. Mladic is hated by Moslems, who call him the "Butcher of Bosnia" for his ruthless attacks.
But unlike his political master, Radovan Karadzic, who fought to remain in the political limelight after the Dayton peace accord was signed a year ago, Mladic virtually disappeared from view.
The Dayton accords demanded that he and other alleged war criminals quit public office and face trial in The Hague.
